clue.text: They cower in subway evacuated by officer stationed with county

indicators.note: a building that is evacuated has had everyone inside removed, so only the outside letters stay

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word, with its contents cleared out
a cop is a police officer
Hants is the standard abbreviation for Hampshire, an English county

explanation.surface: Frightened people shelter in an underground passage, abandoned by a local police officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They cower' looks like the start of a story about frightened commuters, but it is the definition. Hampshire is a county in southern England, usually shortened to Hants.
explanation.definitionFit: Toadies grovel and fawn before the powerful, so cowering servility is their defining habit.

clue.text: Demanding to reveal insiders one’s covering

indicators.note: insiders are those within, so only the interior letters of the word are wanted

blocks.note: Demanding is ASKING; drop its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone insists that people on the inside expose what someone is hiding.
explanation.walkthrough: Demanding means ASKING, and its inner letters spell SKIN. 'Insiders' sounds like people in the know, but it asks for the letters inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The outer layer of tissue wrapping a human body is literally that person's protective coat.

clue.text: Livery company attached to corporation in Kent area

indicators.note: one thing sitting inside another means its letters go within the surrounding pair

blocks.note: Co is the usual abbreviation for company
Kent is in the south-east of England, abbreviated SE
a corporation is jocular slang for a pot belly, a tum

explanation.surface: One of the City of London's livery companies is tied to a corporation based in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points at the old London livery companies and the City Corporation; in fact 'corporation' is an old joke word for a big belly, TUM. Kent is a county in south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Livery is distinctive clothing worn by servants or members of a guild, a kind of uniform outfit.

clue.text: King’s taken in by virtual US president — it’s funny for some

indicators.note: something taken in by another is absorbed into it, so it goes inside

blocks.note: virtual in the sense of being so in effect, practically
Joe Biden, US president
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A monarch is fooled by a near-president, which some people find amusing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Virtual US president' reads as one phrase, but 'virtual' supplies PRACTICAL and the president is JOE (Biden), who holds K.
explanation.definitionFit: A prank played on someone is amusing to the prankster and onlookers, though seldom to the victim.

clue.text: Wavering, making a gamble

blocks.note: taken as written
in British slang a small casual bet, such as on a horse race

explanation.surface: Someone hesitates while placing a bet.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a 'flutter' is a small casual bet, such as on a horse race.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in a state of nervous excitement is to flicker and tremble, so the adjective describes quivering agitation.

clue.text: Smack or junk, glue or speed — any one’s head will roll after time

indicators.note: a head that rolls is lost, and a replacement comes in its place from the next word

blocks.note: junk is WASTE, glue is PASTE, speed is HASTE: any of the three works
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A list of street drugs, heroin, junk, glue and speed, with a warning that someone will lose their job before long.
explanation.walkthrough: Smack, junk and speed all look like drug slang, but 'Smack' is the definition. Each of WASTE, PASTE and HASTE loses its first letter for T.
explanation.definitionFit: A smack of something is a flavour or slight trace of it, the same as a hint on the palate.

clue.text: What mayor returned regularly must take?

definitions.text: What mayor returned regularly must take?

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept and the rest skipped
to return is to go back, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: the even letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Asks what a newly elected civic leader, returned to office again and again, has to swear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returned' suggests re-election, but it reverses the alternate letters of the first two words. The whole clue is also the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking office requires a formal sworn promise, which any mayor must make each time elected.

clue.text: Import less than half of tobacco untarred

indicators.note: taking under half of a run of letters means a short stretch lifted out from within it

blocks.note: seven consecutive letters from fifteen, straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A trade note on bringing in tobacco that has not been tarred.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Import' looks like a trade verb about tobacco shipments; it is the noun meaning significance, as in 'of no account'.
explanation.definitionFit: Import means importance or consequence, and something of no consequence is said to be of little worth or standing.

clue.text: Job done for Stubbs, with a certain power

blocks.note: first meaning: George Stubbs was an English painter famous for his pictures of horses
second meaning: pulled along by an animal, as a cart or carriage is

explanation.walkthrough: George Stubbs (1724-1806) was the great English painter of horses, so a horse sketched is one of his jobs done. The second reading is the ordinary adjective for a carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A carriage moved by animal muscle has the beast as its engine, and a painted steed is one Stubbs completed.

clue.text: Left follows Soviet leader in shifting to far left position

indicators.note: letters shifting to the far left are moved from the back to the very front
to follow is to come after, so this letter is placed at the end

blocks.note: Joseph Stalin, leader of the Soviet Union
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A political note on a party moving toward the hard left after its Soviet leader.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'in' looks like a preposition but names the letters IN, which move from the end of STALIN to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To position something is to set it in place, just as one fits or sets up equipment.

clue.text: Motor ace dismounted the wrong way, carrying something for passenger

indicators.note: going the wrong way means running backwards, so the letters are read right to left
the words carry the answer within them as cargo

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word into the third

explanation.surface: A champion motorcyclist falls off going the wrong way round the track while carrying a pillion.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites a search for a racing driver or a rider; the answer is simply lying backwards inside the opening three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-wheeled carriage bolted to a motorcycle is built to carry a single rider beside the driver.

clue.text: MLK eats in — cafe guy doesn’t have one clean glass?

indicators.note: to eat is to take something inside oneself, so the outer letters swallow the next ones
lacking something means it is removed from the word

blocks.note: Martin Luther King is often called Dr King
taken as written
a man serving tables in a cafe
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A civil rights leader dines indoors, but the waiter at the cafe can't find him a clean glass.
explanation.walkthrough: MLK is Martin Luther King, the doctor of divinity known as Dr King. WAITER without its I gives WATER.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass of safe, potable liquid fit to swallow is clean in the sense of uncontaminated; the question mark flags the loose phrasing.

clue.text: Doing article connected with Lilliputian novel

blocks.note: what are you up to? means what are you doing
the definite article
the Lilliputians of Gulliver's Travels are tiny

explanation.surface: Writing a piece about a Swiftian novel, Gulliver's Travels.
explanation.walkthrough: With Lilliputian in the clue, 'novel' looks like a book; it is the adjective meaning new. Minute here is the adjective for tiny.
explanation.definitionFit: Something novel is fresh and current, of the very latest fashion or information.

clue.text: View of bear on headland

blocks.note: to bear something is to put up with or stand it
a point is a promontory jutting into the sea

explanation.surface: A sighting of a bear standing on a coastal cliff.
explanation.walkthrough: The bear is the verb, meaning tolerate, not the animal. In a down clue, 'on' places the first part above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A view in the sense of an opinion is the position from which one sees an issue.

clue.text: Manchester in need of graduate to regenerate waterways

indicators.note: needing something means being without it, so those letters are missing
regenerating rebuilds something in a new form, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written
an MA is a Master of Arts graduate

explanation.surface: Manchester, needing graduates, plans to restore its canals.
explanation.walkthrough: Manchester is famous for its canals, which makes 'waterways' look like part of the story, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Long narrow ditches can carry water away, so drainage channels are a loose kind of watercourse.

clue.text: Curry, maybe fish starter with rice

indicators.note: a starter comes first, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: skate is a flat fish
the first letter

explanation.surface: A menu: a curry, perhaps with a fish starter and rice.
explanation.walkthrough: Curry is not the dish but John Curry, the British figure skater who won Olympic gold in 1976. 'Starter' sounds like a menu course.
explanation.definitionFit: John Curry was a champion on ice, an example of someone who glides on blades.

clue.text: Woodland pig half falling down on concrete

indicators.note: one half dropping down below the other swaps the two halves round
in a down clue, sitting on something means placed above it

blocks.note: a boar is a male pig
concrete in the sense of actual, tangible

explanation.surface: A wild pig in a wood collapses onto a concrete surface.
explanation.walkthrough: Concrete looks like the building material but means real. Woodland is used as an adjective here.
explanation.definitionFit: Arboreal means relating to trees or living among them, the adjective sense of the forest word.

clue.text: Illegal delivery taken before dance, turned on

indicators.note: something turned round faces the other way, so its letters run backwards
coming before means placed in front of the next part

blocks.note: taken as written
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: Someone takes illegal drugs before going dancing and gets excited.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a no-ball is a delivery by the bowler that breaks the rules, for example overstepping the crease, and gives the batting side a run.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket bowler's throw that breaks the rules is called by the umpire as an invalid ball.

clue.text: Lit up joint in garden

indicators.note: one thing inside another means its letters go within the outer ones

blocks.note: a garden bed where plants grow
a link is a joint or connection, as in a chain

explanation.surface: Someone lit a cannabis joint out in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as smoking a joint; 'Lit up' is the definition and 'joint' is a connecting part.
explanation.definitionFit: A flashing beacon or warning light that switched on briefly and went off again has flickered on and off.

clue.text: Logo used by lecturer’s distinguished contemporary

indicators.note: a lecturer delivers words by speaking, so this piece is what is heard

blocks.note: a brand is a company's identifying mark
to distinguish right from wrong is to know it, so distinguished is KNEW

explanation.surface: An emblem adopted by a university lecturer's eminent colleague of the same generation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Distinguished' looks like praise for a peer; it is the verb, meaning told apart or knew. 'Contemporary' seems to mean a colleague but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Contemporary as an adjective means modern and current, and the answer describes something fresh out of its packaging.

clue.text: Iran manoeuvred to restrict transport and peace

indicators.note: manoeuvring moves pieces into new places, so the letters are rearranged
restricting something hems it in, so these letters surround the other piece

blocks.note: taken as written
a van is a vehicle for transport

explanation.surface: Iran manoeuvres diplomatically to limit shipping while pursuing peace.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like geopolitics; Iran is just four letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: In Buddhism this is the ultimate state of calm and freedom from desire, hence perfect tranquillity.

clue.text: Warrior’s pen represented capturing of adversary?

indicators.note: something re-presented is set out again in a new form, so the letters change order
to capture is to hold inside, so the outer letters enclose the next piece

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A soldier's writing depicts the capture of an enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as loose: the answer is an enemy fighter, taken captive.
explanation.definitionFit: A captured enemy soldier held for the duration of hostilities is an opponent in custody, hence the questioning mark.

clue.text: Added energy by revolutionary technique

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: E is the symbol for energy
by as in multiplied by, the times sign
art is skill or technique

explanation.surface: Fresh energy injected through a radical new method.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' looks like a link but is the multiplication sign, as in three by four.
explanation.definitionFit: Added things are additional or supplementary, over and above the usual amount.

clue.text: Turner in the ascendant, everything’s exhibited

indicators.note: in a down clue, going upward means reading the letters from bottom to top
something exhibited is on display within the words

blocks.note: four consecutive letters from the middle of the word

explanation.surface: With J M W Turner's reputation rising, every one of his paintings is on show.
explanation.walkthrough: Turner looks like the painter, as does 'exhibited'; it is just something that turns. Note the British spelling for a wheel's rubber covering.
explanation.definitionFit: The rubber ring on a wheel rotates as the vehicle moves, so it is something that revolves.

clue.text: Most blackened sink, i.e. stained inside

indicators.note: something inside is contained within the words before it

blocks.note: seven consecutive letters across the three words

explanation.surface: The filthiest sink, i.e. the one with stains inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stained' looks like an anagram signal but is part of the run of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ink makes things dark, so the superlative of the adjective describes whatever is darkest and most smudged.

clue.text: Street in Brussels with a railway opening

indicators.note: one thing inside another means its letters go within the outer ones

blocks.note: Brussels is the seat of the European Union
St is the abbreviation for street
taken as written
Ry is an abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A street in the Belgian capital where a new railway is being opened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' looks like an inauguration; it is the noun, the wide mouth of a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A river's mouth where it widens to meet the sea is a gap through which it empties.

clue.text: Maybe arrange a paper round — one should roll up twice a day

definitions.text: one should roll up twice a day

indicators.note: turning something round makes it face the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: editing is arranging the contents of a newspaper; 'maybe' marks it as one example

explanation.surface: Organising a newspaper delivery round for a youngster, who should turn up twice daily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paper round' suggests a delivery job, but 'round' turns the word back. In Britain a paper round is a child's newspaper delivery route.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea rises up the shore roughly every twelve hours, so it rolls in twice daily.

clue.text: Perfect end or absurd end to episode?

indicators.note: the end of something is its final part, so the last letter is kept

blocks.note: a tail is the end of something
taken as written
mad meaning crazy, absurd
the last letter

explanation.surface: Asks whether a TV episode had a perfect ending or a ridiculous one.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'end' is a piece meaning TAIL; the second 'end' is a selector for the last letter of 'episode'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something made to measure fits its purpose exactly, so it is ideal or just right.
